query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating an actively‐learned moment tensor potential (AL‐MTP) with an analytical entropy correction scheme into free‐energy evaluations will accurately capture the vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions in both solid and liquid phases, thereby substantially reducing computational cost compared to explicit ab initio MD while preserving fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic fidelity.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloy systems near their melting points.
generation.intervention: Replace explicit ab initio molecular dynamics free-energy evaluation with a computational workflow that uses an actively‐learned moment tensor potential trained on finite-temperature ab initio snapshots along with a tailored analytical entropy correction to account for vibrational and anharmonic effects.
generation.conditions: Test the method on binary alloys and then extend to high-entropy (multicomponent) alloy systems, focusing on the temperature range around the fusion point (approximately 0.8–1.2 times the fusion temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: The machine-learned potential energy surface that encodes the relevant vibrational and anharmonic features, including approximated electron–vibration coupling effects, serves as the structural mediator between atomic configurations and free-energy calculations.
generation.mechanism: The AL-MTP, by interpolating the ab initio free-energy landscape with active learning, captures the detailed structural responses (including anharmonic and some electron-vibration effects) without the need to sample an enormous configurational space, while the entropy correction scheme compensates for residual free-energy contributions that are critical for the phase transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion temperatures, latent heat, and free-energy differences predicted by the AL-MTP based workflow should agree within approximately 10% of explicit AIMD results, with computational cost reduced by roughly one order of magnitude relative to AIMD, and with improved scalability over TOR-TILD in multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit, fully-converged ab initio molecular dynamics free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD predictions for fusion properties.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to be valid for alloys where vibrational and anharmonic entropy contributions dominate near the fusion temperature, especially in binary systems and up to the compositional complexity of high-entropy alloys; its accuracy in systems with extreme electron–vibration coupling remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The transferability of the machine-learned potential in capturing subtle electron–vibration interactions and its performance in systems with very high anharmonicity remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative binary alloy and a high-entropy alloy near their melting points. Use both the new AL-MTP plus entropy correction workflow and full explicit AIMD simulations to compute phase free energies and derived fusion observables. The test should include benchmarking the computed fusion temperature, latent heat, and volume change at melting.
measurements: Absolute free energy differences between solid and liquid phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AL-MTP based method yields fusion properties that deviate by more than 10% from those obtained via explicit AIMD, or if the reduction in computational cost is less than an order of magnitude relative to AIMD, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Ab initio framework for deciphering trade-off relationships in multi-component alloys

Abstract: While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. Effect of Ta addition on the structural, thermodynamic and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNi high entropy alloys†

Abstract: Ta addition has considerable effects on the microstructures and mechanical performances of CoCrFeNi alloy systems. Structure search with the special quasirandom structure method and structure identification with first-principles calculations were carried out to investigate the structural, thermodynamic and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNiTax (x = 0.0–1.0) high-entropy alloys in the fcc and bcc lattice frameworks. The predicted lattice parameters of identified structures are in agreement with available experiments. Phase transition between the fcc and bcc lattices was predicted for the lowest-energy structures with increasing Ta content. The predicted temperature dependence of specific heat capacity for the identified structures matches well with the Dulong–Petit, Kepp and Debye Models. Both vibration and configuration entropy contribute to the stabilization of alloy systems, while the latter is about 2–3 times greater than the former.
